title: The Prologue & Chapter One
collection: The Life of St Andrew the Fool

pairs.en: I am about to tell you the life of a man of great virtue. Gather yourselves, I beg you, and listen. What I have to say is a thing that drips honey — a fragrance and a sweetness past all wondering.

So, my children, make your hearts large and ready for the joy of it. Do that, I ask you, and I too will be carried further into the work I have taken up, and I will set before you this man's great deeds of the spirit.
This, then, is how the account begins, of how the wonderful man made his start.

sections.heading: Chapter One — Andrew's service, and the vision

pairs.en: *Andrew's servitude and his willingness to learn.* *The occasion of a holier life.* *The vision.*

**2.** In the reign of Leo the Great, the emperor who loved Christ, there was a man in Constantinople named Theognostos. The devout emperor had honoured him with the rank of protospatharios — a senior title at the imperial court — and in the end he was made a general in the eastern provinces.
This man already owned many household servants, and he bought others as well. One of those he bought was the man our poor pen is now hurrying to praise. He was a Scythian by birth.

From the day his master bought him, along with the rest, he showed himself more teachable than any of them. He was also strikingly good-looking, so much so that his master was thoroughly pleased with him, kept him where he could see him, and used him for whatever he needed. Without wasting any time, Theognostos sent him to be taught the sacred Scriptures — though he could not yet even speak Greek.

The boy had a clear, sober mind, and he quickly learned everything his teacher put in front of him of the things of God. He learned the language of the place as well — Greek, I mean — so fast that his teacher was astonished at how quickly he understood. In time he became the finest of the notaries; and when he was taken away from the schoolroom, he served his master as his secretary. From then on the boy waited on his master with such care and such eagerness that he came to be loved — by his master, by his mistress, and by everyone else in the household.

**3.** Theognostos showed him more and more kindness, taking a particular interest in him and giving him his own cast-off clothes, so that people who saw Andrew would remark that the servant went better dressed than his master.

He was constantly at church too — truly, you could not satisfy him. He loved to read the accounts of what the holy martyrs had suffered, and still more the lives of the men who had carried God within them. He loved them so much that his heart caught fire with a bright longing for them, and he could not help being stirred to imitate them.

So he set his own beginning to a good way of life, and this is how he first began to serve God. One night he got out of bed, in imitation of the saints, to pray at midnight. The cunning demon, seeing the young man's fine start and grudging it, came up and began hammering at the doors of the room he was living in with a terrifying crash. The young man was seized with fear, left off his prayer, hurried back into bed and hid himself under his goat's-hair blankets.

**4.** Fear gave way to the deepest sleep, and there the blessed man saw this. He was in a theatre. On one side of it stood a vast crowd of Ethiopians, an unbearable gathering; on the other, a crowd of men in white, dignified and holy to look at.

The two sides were arguing with each other about a race and a wrestling match. The Ethiopians had a huge Moor with them, and they were demanding of the company in white: *Who is going to run and wrestle against this man of ours?* No one had ever stood up to him, they said — though he had grappled with a great many, since the beginning of the world. He was, in fact, the commander of a thousand in that great legion of Satan.
While they were boasting like this, and Andrew stood there listening, and the men in white were at a loss, a young man of great beauty came down from above. He held three crowns in his hand.

The first was covered in flowers and worked in pure royal gold. The second had priceless stones and pearls set all round it and on both sides, flashing like stars. The third was larger than the other two: it was woven out of every kind of bloom — roses, lilies, plants and branches from the paradise of God — so that it could never wither, and it carried a fragrance no human mind could describe.

**5.** Seeing all this, Andrew ached with longing, turning over how on earth he might get even one of those crowns. He went up to the beautiful young man and said: *As you hope to have Christ — tell me, are these for sale?* *I dare say I can afford them.* *Only bear with me a moment: I will go and tell my master, and he will give you as much gold as you want, and you can take it.*

The young man smiled at him and said: *Believe me, my friend, if you brought me all the gold in the world I would not hand over one of these flowers — not to you, not to anybody else, and certainly not to the man you call your master.* *These do not belong to this empty world, as you supposed.* *They are treasures of heaven, the crowns of Christ, and they are set on the heads of those who strike down those Moors.* *If you want, not one of them but all three — go and wrestle that soot-black Ethiopian.* *Beat him, and you will carry off not only these but as many more as you like, and far more beautiful ones, from my hand.*
At those words Andrew took heart, and said to him: *Believe me, I will do what you say.* *Only teach me his tricks.*

The young man said: *Do you really not know this?* *The Ethiopians are all bluster and no courage — rotten through and don't have the strength.* *Don't let the sheer size of him alarm you: he is as soft as a garden vegetable, rotten and powerless.*

He said this and a good deal more to rub courage into the young man, like oil into a wrestler. Then the beautiful young man took hold of him as though wrestling with him, and showed him how to stand against the Ethiopian. At the end he said into his ear: *When he lifts you off your feet and swings you round — and I know he will — don't panic.* *Lock yourself against him in the shape of a cross, and you will see the glory of God.*

**6.** So the blessed man went out into the middle to wrestle, and stood facing the Ethiopian, and called out at the top of his voice: *Come on then, you soot-black, miserable, useless thing — let the two of us wrestle.*

The Ethiopian heard it and came at a run, snorting and blustering, seized Andrew and swung him round and round for a horrible long time — so that the Ethiopians clapped for joy and the men in white groaned. They thought the Moor would dash him to the ground and knock the eyes out of his head. But as he was being swung, Andrew locked himself against him in the shape of a cross and threw him to the ground. The demon's skull happened to strike a rock; he went straight down and never made another sound.

Then a great burst of applause went up from the men in white, and the sweetest joy; they caught the blessed man up high on their open palms, and every one of them kissed him and anointed him with the fragrant oils of the Spirit. All those Moors were scattered and slunk off in deep disgrace.
The beautiful young man made him a present of the spotless crowns, and Andrew was overjoyed to wear them, for an overwhelming fragrance came off them. Then he embraced him and said:

*Go, and go well.* *From this moment you are one of us — my friend, and my dearest brother.* *So run the good race stripped for it.* *Become a fool for my sake.* *And on the day of my kingdom you will sit as master of many good things.*
